name: Recrystallisation
kb: Purification by dissolving in hot solvent and cooling to form pure crystals
note: Not dissolution plus evaporation, but controlled cooling: the key is knowing exactly when mother liquor will release only the pure crystal. Impurities stay dissolved or crystallise at different temperatures. Each substance needs a different solvent.

name: Sublimation apparatus
kb: Direct phase change from solid to gas, without melting
note: A cold finger condenses the vapour. The apparatus must be absolutely sealed and the heating exact. Used for camphor, naphthalene, iodine. Quality difference: crude apparatus gives degradation, proper cooling finger does not.

name: Reflux condenser
kb: Liquid boils, condenses on cooling finger, returns to pot. Solvent does not escape.
note: The discovery is that you can heat a reaction indefinitely without losing solvent. Allows long reactions at controlled temperature. The cooling finger must be of the right dimensions to balance condensation rate with back-pressure.

name: Soxhlet extractor
kb: Solvent condenses, fills siphon chamber, auto-empties. Repeats hundreds of times. Exhausts the solid.
note: The siphon is the invention: gravity triggers emptying at exactly the right moment, so the same solvent portion hits fresh solid repeatedly. Extracts far more than single contact. The glass siphon tube is the critical precision piece.

name: Steam distillation
kb: Bubbling steam through solid or liquid, carrying volatile oil, then condensing the mixture
note: Works at boiling point of water, not the boiling point of the oil, so thermally labile compounds survive. The product is an emulsion of oil and water; separation requires decanting or salting out. Standard for essential oils.

name: Vacuum distillation
kb: Distillation at reduced pressure lowers boiling point and prevents thermal decomposition
note: A liquid that decomposes at 250 C can be distilled at 100 C under half-bar vacuum. Requires a pump that does not introduce oil vapour, else contamination. The condenser must be cold; ice bath is standard.

name: Azeotropic distillation
kb: Adding a third liquid to break a constant-boiling mixture
note: Ethanol and water form an azeotrope at 96 per cent ethanol; cannot be separated by ordinary distillation. Adding benzene shifts the azeotrope and allows anhydrous ethanol to be drawn off. Requires knowing what the azeotrope is for your pair.

name: Fractional crystallisation
kb: Crystallising mixtures at different temperatures to separate compounds by solubility difference
note: The key is knowing the solubility curve of each substance versus temperature. One compound might dissolve at 20 C but not at 5 C; another the reverse. Cooling in stages, filtering each crop, and recrystallising each fraction purifies both.

name: Dialysis through parchment
kb: Small dissolved molecules pass through parchment; large molecules do not
note: Used to separate salts from proteins, or colloids from small ions. The driving force is diffusion; it is slow. A bag of parchment filled with solution, immersed in water, leaches out the small ions while keeping the colloid inside.

name: Electrophoresis in gelatin
kb: Charged molecules move through a gel toward the electrode of opposite charge
note: The gel is gelatin or agar. A steady voltage is applied. Different proteins move at different speeds depending on their net charge and mass. Requires a stable voltage source and knowledge that the gel must be pH-controlled.

name: Paper chromatography
kb: Liquid solvent carries dissolved compounds up paper at different rates, separating them
note: Paper acts as the stationary phase; the solvent is the mobile phase. Compounds separate by their affinity for each. Spot the mixture at the bottom, suspend in a jar with solvent in the bottom, the liquid wicks up. Each compound travels to a different height.

name: Column chromatography
kb: Solvent flows down a column of adsorbent, carrying compounds at different speeds
note: The column is a glass tube packed with finely ground adsorbent. Solvent drips down slowly; compounds emerge at different times. The invention is realising that flow rate, particle size, and solvent polarity are the controlling parameters. Carbon or silica work; choice changes the separation.

name: Gas chromatography
kb: Carrier gas flows through a heated column. Vapours of different compounds emerge at different times.
note: The column is filled with an adsorbent or liquid on an inert support, heated to 200 C or more. The sample vaporises and passes through. Each compound sticks and releases at a different temperature, detected as it emerges. Requires precise temperature control.

name: Ion exchange resin
kb: Resin beads swap ions with the solution, removing one ion and adding another
note: A resin carries fixed negative or positive charges on its skeleton. Mobile counterions in the pores swap with ions in the solution. Allows softening water, concentrating rare ions, or fully deionising. Capacity is finite; resin is regenerated by reversing the swap.

name: Liquid-liquid extraction
kb: Shaking a solution with an immiscible solvent transfers target compounds to the new phase
note: Water and ether do not mix. If you dissolve a salt in water and shake it with ether, some salts transfer to the ether layer. The degree of transfer depends on solubility in each solvent. Repeat extraction exhausts the aqueous phase.

name: Centrifuge
kb: Spinning a solution accelerates settling of suspended particles by artificial gravity
note: A rotating bucket or rotor creates artificial gravity, accelerating sedimentation a thousand-fold. Particles settle in seconds instead of hours. The tube must be strong; high-speed breakage is dangerous. Design of rotor balance is critical.

name: Freeze-drying apparatus
kb: Freezing aqueous solution then evaporating ice under vacuum without melting
note: The sample is frozen solid, then pressure is reduced to perhaps 10 pascals. Ice sublimes directly to vapour without passing through liquid. Preserves heat-sensitive compounds and yields an airy powder. Requires a condenser to capture the water vapour.

name: Gravimetric analysis
kb: Isolating and weighing a pure compound to determine the original amount of an element
note: E.g. to find sulphur in coal, burn it to SO2, absorb in base to form sulphate, precipitate as BaSO4, filter, dry and weigh. The mass of BaSO4 multiplied by the ratio of atomic weights gives the original sulphur. Accuracy depends on pure precipitate.

name: Titrimetry and burettes
kb: Slowly adding a reagent of known concentration until an endpoint colour change occurs
note: A burette is a long glass tube with a glass stopcock at the bottom, graduated in millilitres. The taper and stopcock must be precise or the burette leaks or sticks. The endpoint must be sharp and visible. Success depends on indicator choice and technique.

name: Acid-base indicators
kb: Dyes that change colour sharply at specific pH values, used to detect endpoints
note: Methyl orange is red below pH 3.1, yellow above. Methyl red is red below pH 4.4, yellow above. Phenolphthalein is colourless below pH 8.2, pink above. Each substance needs the right indicator; choosing wrong gives an error. The indicator must not react with the analyte.

name: Redox titration
kb: Titrating with an oxidising or reducing agent whose colour change marks the endpoint
note: Permanganate solution is deep purple; at the endpoint a tiny excess gives a pink colour that does not fade. Dichromate must have an indicator. Works for any species that oxidises or reduces. The reaction must go to completion and must be fast.

name: Complexometric titration
kb: Titrating with a chelating agent that binds metal ions; indicator changes when metal is bound
note: A chelating agent like EDTA binds metal ions very tightly. The metal indicator dye also binds the metal but less tightly, so EDTA displaces it, changing colour. Works for calcium, magnesium, zinc, etc. Requires careful control of pH.

name: Kjeldahl nitrogen method
kb: Digesting organic matter in sulphuric acid to convert nitrogen to ammonium, then distilling and titrating
note: The sample is heated with conc. H2SO4 and copper sulphate. The high temperature carbonises the sample and oxidises nitrogen to NO, which forms (NH4)2SO4. Ammonia is driven off by distillation with base and collected in acid, then back-titrated. Very robust method.

name: Combustion analysis of organics
kb: Burning organic compound in oxygen, absorbing CO2 and H2O, weighing them to find C and H
note: A weighed sample is combusted in a hot copper tube with oxygen. Products pass through a drying agent, absorbing water in one bulb, then through base, absorbing CO2 in another. Weighing each gives moles of H and C. Requires a furnace at 800-900 C and precise temperature control.

name: Flame photometry
kb: Spraying a solution into a flame and measuring the colour of light emitted by the metal ions
note: Each metal emits light at a characteristic wavelength when heated in a flame. Sodium is orange, potassium is lilac, lithium is red. The intensity depends on concentration. A diffraction grating or prism isolates each wavelength. Highly selective and sensitive.

name: Colorimetry
kb: Comparing the colour intensity of a solution to a standard, or measuring absorbance
note: A coloured compound absorbs light. The more concentrated, the darker the colour. Using a standard solution of known concentration, an unknown can be estimated by colour matching. Or pass light through both and compare intensities. Requires consistent lighting.

name: Spectrophotometry
kb: Measuring light absorbance at specific wavelengths to determine concentration
note: A prism or grating isolates a narrow band of wavelengths. The solution is placed in a cuvette and light is passed through. The transmitted light is measured by a photoelectric cell or photographic plate. The absorbance at each wavelength reveals the identity and concentration.

name: Polarography
kb: Applying a slowly increasing voltage to an electrode in solution; current flow begins when ions are reduced
note: A dropping mercury electrode hangs in the solution. As voltage sweeps from negative to positive, each reducible ion accepts electrons at its characteristic voltage, creating a current pulse. A chart records current versus voltage, showing each ion's reduction potential. Quantitative and selective.

name: Glass pH electrode
kb: A thin glass membrane that responds to hydrogen ion concentration, generating a voltage
note: A special glass is formulated; thin membrane prevents error from water penetration while allowing ion exchange at the surface. The voltage across the membrane varies linearly with pH. Requires a reference electrode and a high-impedance amplifier to measure the tiny current.

name: Conductometry
kb: Measuring electrical conductivity of a solution to determine salt concentration
note: A small AC voltage is applied across two electrodes immersed in the solution. The current depends on the concentration and mobility of ions. Conductivity can titrate; as a precipitate forms, conductivity drops sharply at the endpoint.

name: Refractometry
kb: Measuring refractive index of a solution to determine composition
note: Light bends at different angles depending on the refractive index of the medium. Dissolved substances change the refractive index. A refractometer measures the critical angle of total internal reflection. The value depends on temperature and concentration of solutes.

name: Melting point determination
kb: The temperature at which a pure solid melts is a physical constant that identifies the substance
note: A sample is placed in a capillary tube and heated slowly in a bath or over a flame. The temperature is recorded when the solid first liquefies. Pure substances have sharp melting points; impurities lower and broaden the melting point. Used as a purity test.

name: Contact process for H2SO4
kb: Oxidising SO2 to SO3 over a catalyst, then absorbing in water to make H2SO4
note: The reaction SO2 + O2 -> SO3 is an equilibrium; high temperature drives it backwards. Using a catalyst at 400-450 C allows good conversion without decomposition. Direct absorption of SO3 in water is violent; dilute acid is recycled instead. Cheaper than lead chamber for large scale.

name: Deacon process for Cl2
kb: Oxidising HCl to Cl2 with air over a heated catalyst
note: The reaction 4 HCl + O2 -> 2 Cl2 + 2 H2O is thermodynamically downhill but slow. A copper or iron oxide catalyst at 400-450 C makes it practical. Exhaust gases must be cooled and absorbed in alkali to recover unreacted HCl, else losses are severe.

name: Castner-Kellner process
kb: Electrolyzing NaOH solution with a flowing mercury cathode to produce Cl2 and NaOH without contamination
note: Unlike the diaphragm cell, the mercury cathode prevents Cl2 and NaOH from mixing. Sodium dissolves in mercury, forming an amalgam, then is reacted with water in a separate vessel to produce NaOH and H2. Yields high-purity product. Capital cost and mercury loss are high.

name: Bayer process for alumina
kb: Digesting bauxite in hot NaOH, filtering, acidifying, and calcining to obtain pure Al2O3
note: Bauxite contains silica, iron oxide and alumina. In hot NaOH solution, alumina dissolves as sodium aluminate while silica and iron stay behind. Filtering, cooling and seeding precipitates Al(OH)3, which is filtered and calcined. SiO2 contamination ruins the process; careful ore selection matters.

name: Frasch process for sulphur
kb: Injecting hot water and compressed air into underground sulphur deposits, liquefying it, and pumping to surface
note: Sulphur has a melting point of 115 C. Superheated water (160 C) injected through a pipe liquefies it. Compressed air lifts the liquid sulphur to the surface. The trick is the triple concentric pipe: steam goes down the outer annulus, air down the inner tube, liquid sulphur up the middle. Capital is very high.

name: Ostwald process for HNO3
kb: Oxidising ammonia to nitric acid over a platinum gauze, in two stages
note: Ammonia and air are passed over heated platinum at 850 C; ammonia oxidises to NO. NO is cooled and oxidised to NO2 by air. NO2 is absorbed in water, producing HNO3. Platinum is essential; base metals poison the reaction. Yield approaches 95 per cent.

name: Birkeland-Eyde process for NOx
kb: Passing air through an electric arc to produce nitrogen oxides, then absorbing in water for HNO3
note: The arc heats air to 3000 C, causing N2 and O2 to combine to form NO. Cooling quenches the equilibrium, preserving product. Less efficient than Ostwald; main advantage is no catalyst needed, so no contamination risk. Now obsolete due to Ostwald superiority.

name: Cyanamide process
kb: Reacting calcium carbide with nitrogen gas at high temperature to produce calcium cyanamide
note: CaC2 + N2 at 1200 C yields CaCN2. The cyanamide can be hydrolysed to ammonia. This is a way to fix atmospheric nitrogen without needing the Haber process or electricity-intensive methods. Requires cheap calcium carbide.

name: Fischer-Tropsch synthesis
kb: Converting CO and H2 (syngas) over a catalyst to produce liquid hydrocarbons
note: Syngas is produced from coal or oil. The stoichiometry is CO + 2 H2 -> CH2 + H2O. A chain reaction at 200 C and 20 atmospheres over iron or cobalt gives a mixture of alkanes and alkenes, predominantly C8-C20. Water is removed as it forms. Yield is 80-90 per cent carbon.

name: Bergius coal liquefaction
kb: Hydrogenating coal at high temperature and pressure over a catalyst to produce liquid oil
note: Coal and oil are mixed into a paste with a hydrogen donor, heated to 450 C at 200 atm with a catalyst. The coal is hydrogenated and liquefied. Produces 100 litres of liquid per kg of coal at 70 per cent yield. Very high pressure and temperature make the apparatus expensive.

name: Thermal cracking of oil
kb: Heating heavy oil fractions to 700-900 C to break C-C bonds and produce lighter products
note: Visbreaking cracks long chains into shorter ones, lowering viscosity. Full cracking at 800 C gives gasoline and gas-oil. The products are high in alkenes and aromatics. The selectivity is poor; products are complex. Used to increase yield from the crude.

name: Catalytic cracking of oil
kb: Cracking oil over a zeolite or clay catalyst at 500 C, selective for gasoline-range products
note: A solid catalyst cracks oil at lower temperature than thermal cracking, giving better selectivity. The catalyst is regenerated by burning coke off the surface. Main products are gasoline-boiling-range alkenes and aromatics. Economics are better than thermal cracking.

name: Reforming of naphtha
kb: Converting low-octane alkanes to high-octane aromatics and branched alkanes over a catalyst at 500 C
note: Straight-chain alkanes are dehydrogenated and cyclised, forming aromatics. Branched alkanes are formed. The octane number jumps from 50 to 90+. Hydrogen is produced as a by-product. Platinum requires regeneration to remove coke, and catalyst poisons must be removed from feed.

name: Alkylation of aromatic hydrocarbons
kb: Adding alkyl groups to benzene or toluene using a Lewis acid catalyst
note: Benzene and ethylene react over AlCl3 to form ethylbenzene. Toluene and methanol react to form xylene. The reaction is fast and exothermic. Product selectivity depends on catalyst choice and operating conditions. Important for synthetic detergents and solvents.

name: Claus process for sulphur recovery
kb: Converting H2S in refinery tail gas to elemental sulphur by partial oxidation
note: Two-thirds of H2S is oxidised to SO2, one-third stays as H2S. They react at 250 C to form elemental sulphur: 2 H2S + SO2 -> 3 S + 2 H2O. A catalyst is not strictly needed but makes the reaction faster. Multiple stages recover 95 per cent of sulphur.

name: Kraft pulping of wood
kb: Cooking wood chips in hot caustic soda solution to dissolve lignin, leaving cellulose fibres
note: White liquor (NaOH and Na2S) at 170 C and 10 atm dissolves lignin selectively, leaving strong cellulose fibres. Black liquor (the dissolved lignin and spent chemicals) is burned for energy. Recovery of chemicals by crystallisation and calcining closes the cycle. Produces very strong paper.

name: Sulphite pulping of wood
kb: Cooking wood in bisulphite solution at 150 C to dissolve lignin while preserving cellulose
note: SO2 and Ca(OH)2 form calcium bisulphite, which at 150 C breaks C-O bonds in lignin. Cellulose is not attacked. Liquor is not recovered, so chemicals must be replenished. Product is weaker than kraft but easier processing. Pulping liquor can be used for vanillin extraction.

name: Esterification reaction
kb: Condensing an alcohol with a carboxylic acid in the presence of an acid catalyst to form an ester
note: R-COOH + R'-OH <-> R-COO-R' + H2O. Equilibrium is unfavourable; success requires removing water. A condenser refluxes the mixture; water distils off. Conc. H2SO4 acts as both acid catalyst and dehydrating agent. Esters often smell of fruits and are used for flavour.

name: Saponification and soap making
kb: Hydrolyzing fat with alkali to produce glycerol and soap (fatty acid salt)
note: Fats are triglycerides. Hot NaOH breaks the ester bonds, forming glycerol and sodium salts of fatty acids. The sodium salts precipitate from the aqueous solution as soap. Yield is quantitative. The byproduct glycerol is valuable. An old industry now with exact chemistry.

name: Nitration reactions
kb: Substituting NO2 groups onto aromatic rings using nitric acid and sulphuric acid
note: The nitronium cation NO2+ is generated in-situ and attacks the aromatic ring. Each position can be nitrated; mono, di, tri products are possible. Temperature controls selectivity; hot favours ortho/para, cold favours meta. Strongly exothermic; heat removal is critical.

name: Sulfonation reactions
kb: Substituting SO3H groups onto aromatic rings using fuming sulphuric acid
note: Fuming sulphuric acid contains free SO3. At 80-100 C, SO3 attacks the aromatic ring. Multiple sulfonation can occur. Sulfonated aromatics are water-soluble and useful as intermediates for dyes and detergents. The reaction is reversible; dilution with water drives formation.

name: Halogenation of aromatics
kb: Substituting Cl or Br groups onto benzene and derivatives using the halogen and a Lewis acid catalyst
note: Chlorine and AlCl3 form the active electrophile. Iodine requires activation by an oxidiser like HNO3. Ortho/para selectivity depends on temperature and substituents. Each halogenation can be followed by another at a different position. Used widely for making intermediates.

name: Friedel-Crafts acylation and alkylation
kb: Attaching alkyl or acyl groups to aromatic rings using an acylium or alkyl cation generated by Lewis acid
note: AlCl3 activates acyl chlorides to form acylium cations, which attack the aromatic ring. This is how acetophenone and propiophenone are made. Alkylation is similar but uses alkyl halides; requires excess AlCl3 and is harder to control. Acylation is cleaner.

name: Aldol condensation
kb: Condensing two aldehyde or ketone molecules by enolate nucleophilic attack, then dehydrating to unsaturated product
note: Base deprotonates the alpha carbon, forming an enolate carbanion. It attacks the carbonyl carbon of another molecule. The aldol product has OH and can be dehydrated to an alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl. Used to make aromatic aldehydes and complex organic molecules.

name: Grignard reaction
kb: Using an alkyl magnesium halide to nucleophilically attack carbonyls, forming alcohols and amines
note: RMgX is formed by adding alkyl halide to magnesium in dry ether. The Grignard carbanion attacks carbonyls. Formaldehyde gives primary alcohols, aldehydes give secondary, ketones give tertiary. Esters give ketones. Water quench liberates the alcohol. Requires scrupulous dryness.

name: Diazotisation and coupling
kb: Converting aromatic amines to diazonium salts, which couple with aromatic nucleophiles to form azo dyes
note: ArNH2 is treated with nitrous acid (HNO2, generated from NaNO2 and dilute HCl) at 0 C to form ArN2+. This diazonium salt is highly reactive. Coupling with phenol or aniline gives azo compounds, highly coloured. The entire history of synthetic dyes rests on this reaction.

name: Bechamp reduction of nitro compounds
kb: Reducing aromatic nitro compounds to amines using iron powder in acetic acid
note: ArNO2 is suspended in acetic acid with iron powder. Water is added slowly. The iron is oxidised to Fe2+ and Fe3+, which reduce the nitro group stepwise to ArNH2. Much cheaper than catalytic hydrogenation. The amine salt is basified and extracted. Very robust process.

name: Catalytic hydrogenation
kb: Adding hydrogen to unsaturated compounds over a catalyst
note: Hydrogen and the organic compound are passed over nickel or palladium powder or pellets at 100-200 C. Alkenes add hydrogen to form alkanes. Alkynes give alkenes first, then alkanes. Aromatic rings require higher temperatures and pressure. Catalyst selectivity allows controlling which double bond reacts first.

name: Permanganate oxidation
kb: Oxidising organic compounds with potassium permanganate, cold or hot
note: Cold dilute permanganate oxidises alkenes to diols and alkynes to dicarbonyls. Hot permanganate oxidises alcohols to carbonyls and carbonylsto carboxylic acids. Aromatic side chains are oxidised to carboxylic acids. The solution decolourises as it reacts; endpoint is visible. Very versatile.

name: Dichromate oxidation
kb: Oxidising alcohols and aldehydes using acidified potassium dichromate
note: In conc. H2SO4, dichromate oxidises primary alcohols to aldehydes, then to carboxylic acids. Secondary alcohols form ketones. The colour changes from orange to green. Addition of water controls the degree of oxidation. Old, standard method in classical organic chemistry.

name: Addition polymerisation
kb: Polymerising alkenes by adding monomer units across the double bond
note: Ethylene under pressure with a peroxide catalyst at 200 C forms polyethylene. Vinyl chloride forms PVC. Styrene forms polystyrene. The reaction can be free-radical, cationic, or anionic. Temperature and pressure control molecular weight. Molecular weight in the range 5000-100000 is typical.

name: Condensation polymerisation
kb: Polymerising using diol and diacid (or diamine and diacid) with loss of water or HCl
note: Ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid form polyethylene terephthalate (PET). Hexamethylene diamine and adipic acid form nylon-66. Each esterification or amidation releases water. High temperature drives equilibrium forward. Molecular weight can exceed 100000.

name: Vulcanisation of rubber
kb: Crosslinking rubber with sulphur at 150-200 C to form a stiffer, more resilient material
note: Raw rubber is soft and sticky. Heating with sulphur causes the sulphur to react with the double bonds in the polymer chains, forming crosslinks. More sulphur creates more crosslinks, making the rubber harder. Over-vulcanisation embrittles it. Temperature control is critical.

name: Acetic acid production
kb: Oxidising ethanol to acetic acid, using permanganate or dichromate or air over a catalyst
note: Ethanol is oxidised in two steps: to acetaldehyde, then to acetic acid. Air oxidation requires a catalyst like copper or cobalt at 200 C. Permanganate is faster but requires stoichiometric reagent. Old vinegar fermentation is slow but cheap. Used for making acetates and esters.

name: Acetone production
kb: Producing acetone from isopropanol oxidation or cumene process
note: Isopropanol is oxidised by permanganate or dichromate to acetone. Cumene (isopropylbenzene) is oxidised to a hydroperoxide, which rearranges to phenol and acetone. Cumene process is cheaper at large scale. Acetone is a polar solvent and ketone intermediate.

name: Acetylene from calcium carbide
kb: Hydrolyzing calcium carbide with water to produce acetylene gas
note: CaC2 + 2 H2O -> C2H2 + Ca(OH)2. The reaction is vigorous and exothermic; water control is important. Acetylene is a gas at STP, used for welding, lighting, and as a chemical intermediate. Production is simple and scalable. Only needs calcium carbide and water.

name: Methanol synthesis
kb: Synthesising methanol from CO and H2 over a catalyst
note: Syngas (CO + 2 H2) over copper-zinc oxide catalyst at 200-250 C and 50-100 atm yields methanol. The reaction is exothermic and reversible; high pressure and lower temperature favour methanol. Unreacted gas is recycled. Used as solvent and fuel.

name: Diethyl ether synthesis
kb: Condensing two ethanol molecules with loss of water, catalysed by conc. H2SO4 at 140 C
note: Two ethanol molecules condense via their -OH groups: C2H5OH + C2H5OH -> C2H5-O-C2H5 + H2O. The reaction is an equilibrium; boiling off the ether product drives it forward. Conc. H2SO4 absorbs water, aiding equilibrium. Old synthesis, very simple.

name: Chloroform synthesis
kb: Chlorinating acetone or ethanol with hypochlorous acid formed in-situ
note: Acetone is treated with Cl2 and base. Chlorine and base form hypochlorous acid, which chlorinates the methyl group. Haloform reaction cleaves the molecule to chloroform and carboxylate. Or: ethanol with Cl2 over heat gives chloroform. Used as anaesthetic and solvent.

name: Carbon tetrachloride synthesis
kb: Chlorinating methane or carbon disulfide with chlorine gas at high temperature
note: Methane and Cl2 at 250 C form a mixture of chlorinated products. Sequential chlorination: CH4 -> CH3Cl -> CH2Cl2 -> CHCl3 -> CCl4. Selectivity to CCl4 is poor; product separation is needed. Used as solvent for fats and dry cleaning.

name: Phenol production
kb: Producing phenol from cumene hydroperoxide or by hydrolysing chlorobenzene
note: Cumene (isopropylbenzene) is oxidised by air to cumene hydroperoxide, which rearranges in acid to phenol and acetone. Chlorobenzene hydrolyzes with NaOH at 300 C and high pressure. Cumene route is economically better. Phenol is acidic and forms salts with base.

name: Benzene from coal tar
kb: Distilling and refining the benzene fraction from coal tar
note: Coal tar distillation yields light oils containing benzene, toluene, xylene. Fractional distillation separates benzene at 80 C. Washing with sulphuric acid removes impurities. Recrystallisation from cold alcohol gives pure benzene. Industrial scale needs many litres of coal tar.

name: Toluene from coal tar
kb: Distilling and refining the toluene fraction from coal tar
note: Toluene boils at 111 C, separate from benzene at 80 C. Fractional distillation yields toluene of 95 per cent purity. Washing and recrystallisation improves it further. Used for TNT synthesis, solvents, and chemical intermediates.

name: Xylene from coal tar and synthesis
kb: Isolating xylene isomers from coal tar or synthesising from toluene
note: Coal tar contains ortho-, meta-, and para-xylene in roughly equal amounts. Boiling points are close (137-139 C). Separating the isomers requires many distillations or chemical methods. Or: toluene is dimerised over acid to give xylene. The isomers have different properties.

name: Aniline synthesis from nitrobenzene
kb: Reducing nitrobenzene to aniline using iron and acetic acid
note: PhNO2 is reduced by Fe/acetic acid. The iron is oxidised to Fe2+ and Fe3+, which reduce the nitro group stepwise. The aniline salt is basified and extracted. Pure aniline is a colourless liquid but oxidises in air to a dark polymer. Used as intermediate for dyes and pharmaceuticals.

name: Urea synthesis from ammonia
kb: Synthesising urea from ammonia and CO2 at high pressure
note: NH3 and CO2 at 150-200 C and 100-200 atm form ammonium carbamate, which dehydrates to urea at higher temperatures. Water is removed as ammonia and CO2 are recycled. Yield approaches 100 per cent. Urea is used as fertiliser and for making resins.

name: Formaldehyde synthesis
kb: Oxidising methanol to formaldehyde over a silver or copper catalyst
note: Methanol vapour and air over a silver catalyst at 600-700 C form formaldehyde. The reaction is exothermic; heat must be removed. Yield is 90 per cent; unreacted methanol is recycled. Formaldehyde is used for making resins, preservatives, and explosives.

name: Glycerol as soap byproduct and synthetic
kb: Glycerol is produced as a byproduct of soap making and can be synthesised from dihydroxyacetone
note: Saponification of fats produces glycerol along with soap. Glycerol is removed by salting out or distillation. Purity is improved by fractional distillation. Also made by reduction of dihydroxyacetone. Used for lubricants, explosives (nitroglycerin), and sweetness.

name: Citric acid synthesis and fermentation
kb: Producing citric acid by fermentation of sugar with Aspergillus niger or by chemical synthesis
note: A mold ferments glucose, acetate or itaconate to citric acid. Chemical synthesis is complex. Fermentation is practical but requires careful sterile technique and nutrient control. Citric acid is precipitated as the calcium salt, dissolved in H2SO4 to displace Ca2+, and recovered.

name: Celluloid from nitrocellulose
kb: Mixing nitrocellulose with camphor or other plasticiser to make a flexible plastic
note: Nitrocellulose alone is brittle and explosive. Camphor dissolves in it, acting as a plasticiser. The mixture can be molded when warm and hardens on cooling. Used for combs, billiard balls, and early film. Highly flammable.

name: Viscose from cellulose
kb: Dissolving cellulose in NaOH, treating with CS2, then regenerating the cellulose fibre
note: Cellulose + NaOH forms sodium cellulose. Adding CS2 forms sodium cellulose xanthate, which dissolves in dilute alkali to form viscose. Extruding through a spinneret into acid regenerates cellulose fibre. The fibre is strong and used for rayon textiles.

name: Cellulose acetate plastic
kb: Acetylating cellulose with acetic anhydride in the presence of sulphuric acid catalyst
note: Cellulose + acetic anhydride + H2SO4 catalyst gives cellulose acetate. The product is plastic without needing camphor. Less flammable than celluloid. Can be molded when warm. Used for safety film, spectacle frames, and cigarette filters.

name: Bakelite thermosetting resin
kb: Condensing phenol and formaldehyde with ammonia or acid catalyst to form thermosetting resin
note: Phenol and formaldehyde condense under heat and catalyst to form novolac or resole, depending on conditions. The linear polymer is infusible. Adding more formaldehyde and heating crosslinks it into a thermoset. Very hard, good electrical insulator.

name: Urea-formaldehyde resin
kb: Condensing urea and formaldehyde to form a thermosetting resin
note: Urea + formaldehyde + acid catalyst condense to form a linear polymer, then cross-link on further heating. Harder than bakelite, bleached (white), used for electrical fittings, tableware, adhesives for plywood.

name: Polyvinyl chloride (PVC)
kb: Polymerising vinyl chloride by free radical addition
note: Vinyl chloride (CH2=CHCl) is polymerised in water at 50 C with a peroxide initiator. The vinyl chloride monomer must be dry; water causes side reactions. The polymer forms as a suspension. Used as pipes, insulation, upholstery.

name: Polystyrene
kb: Polymerising styrene by free radical or anionic addition
note: Styrene (C6H5-CH=CH2) is polymerised at 60-100 C with a peroxide initiator. The polymer is glassy and hard. Can be molded by injection or extrusion. Foamed polystyrene is used as insulation and packaging.

name: Polyethylene
kb: Polymerising ethylene at high pressure and temperature with peroxide catalyst
note: Ethylene at 150-300 C and 1000+ atm with peroxide catalyst forms low-density polyethylene (LDPE). A dense structure forms at lower pressure over a Ziegler catalyst. Used for bags, films, insulation. The branching in LDPE makes it flexible; linear HDPE is stiffer.

name: Polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA)
kb: Polymerising methyl methacrylate to form a transparent plastic
note: Methyl methacrylate at 50-100 C with peroxide initiator forms clear polymer. Can be injection molded or cast. Much clearer than polystyrene. Used for aircraft windows, signs, sheets. Good chemical resistance.

name: Nylon-66 polyamide fibre
kb: Condensing hexamethylene diamine and adipic acid to form polyamide fibre
note: H2N(CH2)6NH2 and HOOC(CH2)4COOH at 270 C condense with loss of water, forming a linear polyamide. Extruding the molten polymer through a spinneret forms fibres. Nylon is strong, elastic, and used for textiles, hosiery, bristles. Moisture uptake can be significant.

name: Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) polyester
kb: Condensing ethylene glycol with terephthalic acid or ester to form polyester
note: HOCH2CH2OH and HOOC-C6H4-COOH at 260 C with a tin catalyst condense with loss of water. The linear polyester is extruded and solidified. Fibre has good tenacity and chemical resistance. Films are clear and used for flexible packaging.

name: Neoprene synthetic rubber
kb: Polymerising chloroprene to form an elastic rubber with good oil resistance
note: Chloroprene (2-chlorobutadiene) is emulsion polymerised at 40 C. The chlorine substituent enhances oil and flame resistance compared to natural rubber. Vulcanised with sulphur like natural rubber. Used for hoses, seals, weatherstripping.

name: Buna synthetic rubber
kb: Copolymerising butadiene and styrene to form a rubber-like elastomer
note: Butadiene and styrene (about 3:1) are emulsion copolymerised at 5 C. The low temperature gives high yield and longer chains. Vulcanised with sulphur. Slightly harder than natural rubber. Used for tires, belts, and footwear.

name: Silicone polymers
kb: Polymerising organosiloxanes to form silicone oils, rubbers, and resins
note: Dimethyldichlorosilane hydrolyzes to form siloxane monomers, which condense into a polymer chain. The Si-O backbone is very stable. Varying the alkyl groups and cross-linking gives oils, rubbers, or resins. Excellent thermal stability and water repellency.

name: Thermochemistry and Hess's law
kb: Measuring heats of reaction and predicting unknown heats from known ones
note: Hess's law: the heat change depends only on initial and final states, not the path. A simple calorimeter measures temperature change when a reaction occurs in an insulated container. Knowing specific heats allows computing the enthalpy change. Used to predict unfeasible reactions.

name: Chemical kinetics and rate laws
kb: Measuring reaction rates and determining the order with respect to each reagent
note: Rate = k [A]^m [B]^n. The powers m and n are determined experimentally by varying concentrations and measuring initial rates. The rate constant k depends on temperature via the Arrhenius equation. Catalyst lowers activation energy without changing equilibrium.

name: Equilibrium and equilibrium constant
kb: Understanding that reversible reactions reach an equilibrium where forward and reverse rates are equal
note: At equilibrium, K = [products]/[reactants]. Changing concentration, temperature, or pressure shifts the equilibrium to re-establish K. The position of equilibrium is independent of how much starting material you use. This is Le Chatelier principle.

name: Le Chatelier's principle
kb: Shifting equilibrium by changing concentration, temperature, or pressure
note: Increasing concentration of a product shifts equilibrium to the left. Increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction. Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer moles. Understanding this allows controlling yields in large-scale synthesis.

name: Phase rule and phase diagrams
kb: The Gibbs phase rule determines the number of degrees of freedom in a multi-phase system
note: F = C - P + 2. At a triple point, all three phases coexist and no variable can be changed without losing a phase. Binary phase diagrams show how composition and temperature determine the phases present. Used for design of distillations and crystallisations.

name: Colligative properties
kb: Boiling point elevation, freezing point depression, osmotic pressure, and vapour pressure lowering depend only on solute number, not identity
note: Adding 1 mole of solute to 1 kg water raises the boiling point by 0.5 C, lowers the freezing point by 1.9 C, and raises osmotic pressure by 22 atm. This allows determining molecular weights or detecting dissociation of ionic compounds.

name: The mole and Avogadro constant
kb: The mole is the amount of substance equal to the mass in grams numerically equal to the atomic or molecular weight
note: One mole of any gas at STP occupies 22.4 litres. One mole of solute dissolved in 1 litre gives a one-molar solution. The concept allows exact stoichiometric calculations. Without the mole, chemistry would remain a craft without quantitative control.

name: Electrochemical series
kb: Ranking metals and other species by their tendency to lose electrons
note: Magnesium is more easily oxidised than iron, which is more easily oxidised than copper. A more easily oxidised metal reduces a less easily oxidised metal salt. Used to predict reactions and design electrochemical cells. Potentials are measured versus a standard hydrogen electrode.

name: Overpotential and electrode kinetics
kb: The voltage needed to drive an electrochemical reaction is greater than the theoretical voltage because of activation barriers
note: Hydrogen evolution on copper has high overpotential; on platinum it is much lower. This allows electroplating copper onto steel without plating hydrogen gas. Overpotential depends on current density, temperature, and electrode surface.

name: Nernst equation for electrode potential
kb: The potential of a half-cell depends on the concentration of ions and the standard potential
note: E = E0 + (RT/nF) ln Q. At 25 C with log instead of ln: E = E0 + 0.06/n log Q. Used to predict cell voltages under non-standard conditions. When Q = 1, E = E0. When Q > 1, the potential decreases, pushing the reaction backwards.

name: Anodising and anodic oxidation
kb: Electrochemically oxidising a metal anode to form a protective oxide layer
note: Aluminium is the anode, an inert metal is the cathode, and dilute H2SO4 is the electrolyte. Applying voltage oxidises the aluminium surface to Al2O3. The oxide layer is porous and can be dyed. Anodised aluminium resists corrosion far better than bare metal.
